planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed; give plants extra room since the vines spread more than compact bush hybrids.

directions: Chefini was bred by Petoseed and released in 1965 as one of the first hybrid zucchinis to win an AAS award, valued for fruit so deeply dark green it reads almost black under garden light. The vigorous vines spread more than many modern compact hybrids, so give plants extra room or plan on a wider bed than typical bush-type zucchini. Harvest young at 6-8 inches for the most tender skin and flavor, and keep picking every couple of days since the sprawling growth habit hides fruit under the foliage. In Gulf Coast gardens, its early maturity lets gardeners get a harvest in before summer heat and squash vine borer pressure peak.

common_name: Aristocrat Hybrid Zucchini (AAS-Winning Compact Green Zucchini)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil; compact size suits raised beds and small plots.

directions: Aristocrat won an AAS award in 1973 for combining a compact, space-saving bush habit with the kind of dark green fruit color and shape consistency that open-pollinated zucchini of the era could not match. Plants stay under two feet tall, making this a practical choice for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast garden plots where vining winter squash would take over. Water deeply every few days rather than a light daily sprinkle to keep production steady through hot spells, and harvest fruit at 6-7 inches before the skin toughens. Decades after its release it remains available from mainstream seed catalogs, a testament to its enduring garden performance.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost; well suited to large containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Astia is a French-bred bush zucchini selected specifically for container growing and tight garden spaces, with silvery, deeply lobed foliage that makes the compact plant almost as ornamental as it is productive. Fruit sets close to the base of the plant, which keeps harvest easy even in a large pot on a patio, and the smooth, glossy green zucchini are best cut at about 5 inches for peak tenderness. Because it stays under 30 inches across, Astia suits Gulf Coast gardeners who want fresh zucchini without dedicating a full bed to a sprawling vine, and frequent picking keeps the early, prolific plants setting new fruit.

common_name: Cue Ball Squash (Round Pale Green Hybrid Summer Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed; open bush habit works well in raised beds.

directions: Cue Ball is a round-fruited hybrid squash bred as a paler, milder companion to the dark-skinned Eight Ball type, producing pale green fruit mottled with white on an open, upright bush that keeps the golf-ball to billiard-ball-sized squash easy to spot. Harvest at around 3 inches in diameter for the best texture, since the round shape can hide inside the foliage and size up quickly in hot weather. Its resistance to watermelon mosaic virus and zucchini yellow mosaic virus is a real advantage in humid Gulf Coast summers where aphid-spread viruses build up on cucurbits. The compact plant works well in raised beds where a standard vining summer squash would be too sprawling.

common_name: Butterstick Hybrid Squash (Golden-Yellow Straightneck Summer Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into warm, fertile soil; single-stem habit needs less room than sprawling squash types.

directions: Butterstick is a straightneck-type hybrid that carries the zucchini plant's productive, single-stem habit but sets bright golden-yellow, straight-necked fruit instead of green cylinders. Its smooth skin and creamy flesh stay tender at a generous 7-8 inches, giving a bit more forgiveness than crookneck types if a fruit is missed during a hot Gulf Coast picking cycle. Plants bear over a long season with a steady, single-stem habit rather than sprawling widely, so regular spacing in a sunny bed keeps air moving through the foliage. Consistent moisture and twice-weekly harvest keep the plant setting new fruit rather than bottlenecking on a few oversized squash.

common_name: Spineless Beauty Hybrid Zucchini (Commercial-Grade Itch-Free Zucchini)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early; use drip irrigation to help manage mildew in humid climates.

directions: Spineless Beauty is a widely grown commercial-grade hybrid zucchini bred with smooth, nearly spine-free petioles, sparing gardeners the itchy rash that comes from brushing bristly zucchini foliage during harvest. The open, mounding plant sets glossy, speckled medium-green fruit that hold quality even when picked slightly larger than typical zucchini, at 6-8 inches. Because powdery and downy mildew can move fast through humid Gulf Coast gardens, growers should keep foliage dry with drip irrigation and watch closely during rainy spells since this variety carries no built-in mildew resistance. Regular harvest every two to three days keeps the vigorous, heavy-yielding plant productive through the season.

common_name: One Ball Squash (Round Yellow Hybrid Summer Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed; compact size suits succession planting through a long warm season.

directions: One Ball is the bright yellow counterpart to the dark green Eight Ball and pale Cue Ball round squash, bred by Hollar Seeds to round out a trio of billiard-themed globe-shaped summer squash. The vigorous, disease-resistant bush plant sets shiny yellow fruit best picked at 2-3 inches across for the crispest texture and nuttiest flavor, well before the rind toughens. Its resistance to watermelon mosaic virus and zucchini yellow mosaic virus is valuable in warm, humid Gulf Coast gardens where these aphid-vectored viruses are common late-season problems. The compact habit and small mature fruit size make it a good choice for succession planting in raised beds through a long Texas growing season.
